text:
Montessori School to Close Friday; Parents Shocked by Sudden Announcement and Tech-Focused Replacement Plans
Families at the Santa Monica Montessori School were blindsided this week when director Pam Crisman announced that the longtime independent school at 1909 Colorado Avenue will close permanently this Friday, July 10, 2026
Families at the Santa Monica Montessori School were blindsided this week when director Pam Crisman announced that the longtime independent school at 1909 Colorado Avenue will close permanently this Friday, July 10, 2026.
Parent Alex Mulvaney, whose preschooler attends the school, told the Santa Monica Observer that Crisman informed families she could no longer afford to operate the school in its current traditional Montessori model. The location, he said, will be taken over by a national company that plans to emphasize iPads, online learning, and AI-driven instruction.
"The parents were crying, a lot of them, because they depend on this school and they have very little notice," Mulvaney said. He added that many parents, including himself, are deeply concerned that the new approach "would not work for his child or many of the others in the program."
The abrupt timeline has left families scrambling for alternative care and education options with minimal warning. The school has long served toddlers, early childhood (preschool), and elementary students with a hands-on, child-led Montessori philosophy focused on prepared environments and specialized materials.
Limited Public Confirmation So Far
Publicly available information shows the school's executive director listed as Pamela Crisman, who has held the role since 2003. The institution has operated at the Colorado Avenue address for decades, with roots dating back to 1960.
However, as of Wednesday evening, no closure announcement appears on the school's website (montessorischoollosangeles.com) or its Instagram account (@santamonicamontessori), which has continued posting activity into mid-2026. Extensive searches across news sites and social media platforms, including X, turned up no prior reports or parent discussions about this specific closure.
“She told us she was closing the school because she didn't want to drive up here from Carlsbad anymore," said Mulvaney. "And because of financial pressures and she had to take care of her family. But still somehow she would take all the stuff to run another school of hers. I feel betrayed by her lack of communication. "
"I also feel that my trust has been violated. As I trusted her with my daughter who I love with my whole heart. And one before that. "
Broader Context on Montessori Closures
The situation echoes challenges facing many Montessori programs nationwide. Chains such as Guidepost Montessori have closed dozens of locations in recent years amid financial pressures, post-pandemic recovery struggles, high monthly losses, and difficulties sustaining operations. Some closures have been abrupt, leaving families with short notice.
Traditional Montessori education prioritizes tactile, social, and guided experiences for young children. The shift described by Mulvaney toward screen-based and AI-supported models represents a significant departure that has raised questions among some parents about developmental appropriateness for preschoolers.
Montessori schools face distinctive financial pressures stemming from the philosophy's emphasis on high-quality, individualized, hands-on education, combined with broader early childhood education (ECE) sector challenges like rising costs, enrollment volatility, and economic pressures. While many independent Montessori programs thrive through strong community support and careful management, a wave of closures-particularly among scaled chains-highlights vulnerabilities.
What's Next
Mulvaney and other families are now seeking clarity on final operations, any transition support, and options for the fall. The school's public contact remains (310) 829-3551 and [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection).
The *Santa Monica Observer* reached out to the school for official comment but had not received a response by press time. We will continue monitoring this developing story and provide updates as more details emerge from school leadership or affected families.
Parents or community members with additional information are encouraged to contact the Observer.
